articles.headline: Latent Sparse Attention targets the indexer, not the reader, at 10M-token context
articles.dek: Prefrontal AI and ETH Zurich cluster keys in a learned latent space so sparse attention no longer pays a quadratic cost to decide where to look.
body: Sparse attention lets each query read only a few keys, but the authors report that at 10M tokens about 98% of a sparse layer's prefill time goes to the indexer that picks those keys. Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) projects keys into a low-dimensional learned space and groups them with hierarchical (Ward) clustering. Each bucket keeps a centroid and an index table. Queries score clusters rather than every key. The authors say hierarchical search cuts prefill indexing from \(O(T^2)\) to roughly \(O(T\log T)\), where \(T\) is context length.

There are two variants. D-LSA is distilled onto a pretrained model's attention. N-LSA is trained natively, and at 128K tokens it matched full attention's validation loss. Replacing GLM-5.3-Flash's sparse attention with D-LSA sped up attention-layer prefill 22.7x on H200, or 2.2x end to end. On Qwen3.8-27B, one layer ran 72.4x faster than full attention, and whole-model time to first token improved 9.21x.
The limits are real. LSA reduces the cost of finding keys, not of storing them, so the KV cache still grows linearly. Whole-model gains at 512K are close to nil.
articles.why: It shows that at ultra-long context the bottleneck in sparse attention is key selection, which opens a route to subquadratic attention that doesn't give up full-attention accuracy.

terms.def: Lightweight scorer that selects which keys each query attends to in sparse attention.
Inference phase that processes the whole prompt in parallel before generating tokens.

sources.title: Accelerating Attention for Ultra-Long Context (Prefrontal AI)
Latent Sparse Attention: 72x in One Layer, 9x for the Whole Model at 10M Tokens

deeper: Sparse attention replaces the dense softmax over all \(T\) keys with a softmax over a small selected set \(S_i\) per query:

\[
o_i = \sum_{j\in S_i} \frac{\exp(q_i^\top k_j/\sqrt{d})}{\sum_{l\in S_i}\exp(q_i^\top k_l/\sqrt{d})}\, v_j, \qquad |S_i| \ll T.
\]

The attention itself is then cheap. The catch is choosing \(S_i\). Learned indexers score every key for every query, which is \(O(T)\) per query and \(O(T^2)\) over a prefill. The authors report that at 10M tokens this indexer takes about 98% of a sparse layer's prefill time. LSA targets that cost rather than the attention readout.

The mechanism has four steps. First, keys are projected into a low-dimensional learned space, \(z_j = Wk_j \in \mathbb{R}^r\) with \(r \ll d\), so distances are cheap and trained to be useful for retrieval. Second, the projected keys are grouped by Ward hierarchical clustering. Ward merges the pair of clusters \(A,B\) whose union least increases within-cluster variance:

\[
\Delta(A,B) = \frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\,\lVert \mu_A-\mu_B\rVert^2 .
\]

Third, each bucket stores a centroid \(\mu_c\) and an index table listing its member keys. Fourth, a query is projected into the same space and scored against centroids, \(s(q,c)=\tilde q^\top \mu_c\), and the keys of the top-scoring clusters become \(S_i\). Searching the cluster tree top-down, keeping a few branches per level, costs about \(O(\log T)\) per query. That gives the claimed \(O(T\log T)\) prefill indexing instead of \(O(T^2)\).

There are two variants. D-LSA distills the projection and clustering onto a pretrained model's existing attention, so it can retrofit a model. N-LSA is trained natively, and at 128K tokens it matched full attention's validation loss. That is evidence that a clustered index need not cost quality, at least at that length.

Compared with prior approaches, fixed patterns such as windows or blocks are cheap but content-blind. Learned indexers are content-aware but still touch every key. Hashing schemes approximate nearest-neighbor search but use random rather than learned geometry. LSA's pitch is a learned geometry plus a tree, so the search is sublinear in keys.
The reported numbers show how Amdahl's law applies. Swapping D-LSA into GLM-5.3-Flash sped attention-layer prefill 22.7x but end-to-end only 2.2x. With speedup \(s\) on a fraction \(f\) of runtime,
so once the indexer is gone, the MLPs, other layers, and remaining attention dominate. On Qwen3.8-27B, one layer ran 72.4x faster than full attention and time to first token improved

articles.headline: Low-rank output gates make linear-attention baselines stronger, and Canon layers close the rest of the gap
articles.dek: A new 'Physics of Language Models' installment proposes GLA5 and GDN2, which swap a full-rank output gate for a rank-16 one and spend the savings elsewhere.
body: Gated linear attention keeps a matrix-valued recurrent state updated as \[S_t = G_t \odot S_{t-1} + k_t^{\top} v_t,\] with a data-dependent forget gate \(G_t\). The paper, Part 4.2 of the series, targets the output gate. In GLA and Gated DeltaNet that gate can take up to a third of the recurrent layer's parameters. GLA5 and GDN2 replace it with a low-rank gate (rank \(r=16\), value dimension \(d_v=2d\)) and give the freed parameters to the rest of the layer. All linear models are compared under strict parameter alignment.

The result is stronger baselines for both GLA and Gated DeltaNet. Without Canon layers, GDN2 leads GLA5 at every model size. With Canon layers, that lead nearly vanishes. The simpler GLA5 then matches GDN2 and beats Mamba2. This suggests that much of the delta rule's advantage can be recovered by cheaper local mixing. The authors say both designs came out of their synthetic pretraining playground, and the paper's title says they tested them at scale.
articles.why: The parameter-matched comparisons put the recurrent-memory rule (gated accumulation versus delta rule) on a fairer footing, which matters when choosing linear layers for hybrid models.

terms.def: Lightweight local token-mixing layers added alongside attention or recurrent blocks.
Recurrent update that erases the state's prediction for a key before writing the new value.

sources.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale
Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training

deeper: Gated linear attention replaces the growing key-value cache with a fixed-size matrix state \(S_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d_v}\). Each step decays the old state with a data-dependent gate and writes a rank-one outer product:
\[S_t = G_t \odot S_{t-1} + k_t^{\top} v_t, \qquad o_t = q_t S_t.\]

Because the update is linear in \(S\), training can be parallelized over chunks, and inference costs \(O(d_k d_v)\) per token regardless of context length. The layer's output then passes through a separate output gate, roughly \(y_t = W_o\,(o_t \odot \phi(W_g x_t))\) for some nonlinearity \(\phi\). That gate projection is the target of this paper.

With \(d_v = 2d\), a full-rank \(W_g \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_v}\) costs \(2d^2\) parameters. In GLA and Gated DeltaNet this can reach a third of the recurrent layer. The paper factorizes it as \(W_g = AB\), with \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\), \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_v}\) and \(r=16\). That costs \(r(d+d_v)=48d\) parameters, which is linear rather than quadratic in width. The freed budget goes to the rest of the layer, and the resulting variants are GLA5 and GDN2. The comparison is run under strict parameter alignment, so any gain cannot come from a larger model.

The two families differ in how they write to the state. GLA's write is purely additive, so it accumulates associations and relies on decay to forget. Gated DeltaNet uses the delta rule, which first reads what the state currently predicts for \(k_t\) and then corrects the error:

\[S_t = \alpha_t\,(I - \beta_t k_t^{\top}k_t)\,S_{t-1} + \beta_t k_t^{\top} v_t \;=\; \alpha_t\big[S_{t-1} - \beta_t k_t^{\top}(k_t S_{t-1} - v_t)\big] + \beta_t k_t^{\top} v_t \text{ (up to placement of } \alpha_t).\]

This is one step of online gradient descent on \(\tfrac12\|k_t S - v_t\|^2\). It overwrites rather than piles up, which helps associative recall. The cost is a more complex, less trivially parallel kernel.

The empirical story has two parts. Without Canon layers, GDN2 beats GLA5 at every size, which matches the usual view that the delta rule is the stronger mixer. With Canon layers, which add cheap local mixing across neighboring tokens, the gap nearly closes. GLA5 then matches GDN2 and beats Mamba2. A plausible reading is that part of what the delta rule buys is local sharpening of recent key-value structure. A short-range mixer can supply that more cheaply, leaving the recurrent state to carry longer-range content. That is an interpretation, not something the brief establishes.
The practical implication is that the simplest recurrence, once its parameters are allocated well and local mixing is added, may be enough. That would ease kernel design and deployment.
There are several caveats. Both designs came out of the authors' synthetic pretraining playground, so selection effects are possible, and the title claims scale testing wh

articles.headline: ROAM-GRPO routes solved prompts into self-distillation to stop reasoning collapse
articles.dek: A Caltech-affiliated NeurIPS workshop paper targets the loss of reasoning diversity that RLVR with GRPO tends to cause.
body: SFT followed by RLVR is now the default recipe for reasoning models. It is known to collapse the policy onto one low-diversity solution mode. ROAM-GRPO (Duan and Thomson, arXiv 2611.25926, submitted this week) changes the training loop to counter that. Standard GRPO samples \(G\) completions per prompt and uses the group-normalized advantage \[\hat{A}_i = \frac{R_i - \text{mean}(R_{1:G})}{\text{std}(R_{1:G})}.\]

The paper's approach is to detect prompts that are already well solved. A prompt counts as solved when at least \(k\) of its \(G\) completions are correct. Those prompts leave the GRPO objective and go to an "off-mode" track. There the model is asked for distinct solution strategies. An LLM judge checks each one for logical validity and distinctness. The accepted alternatives are then self-distilled back into the policy.

This spends the saturated prompts, which give near-zero advantage anyway, on exploration instead of more sharpening. The authors' qualitative traces show baseline GRPO sticking to one dominant approach. The ROAM variants attempt several, including some computational shortcuts. A delayed variant that switches on partway through training is also reported. The paper is a short workshop submission and relies on an LLM judge for distinctness, so treat the diversity claims as preliminary.
articles.why: Pass@k and exploration headroom are what RL scaling depends on, and this offers a cheap way to keep diversity without giving up average accuracy.

terms.def: RL narrowing a model's outputs to one dominant solution mode.
Training a model on verified outputs it generated itself.

sources.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining (arXiv abstract)
ROAM-GRPO full text (arXiv PDF)

deeper: Reasoning models are now typically trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The known failure is that RL sharpens the policy onto one solution mode, so pass@1 may improve while diversity shrinks. ROAM-GRPO (Duan and Thomson, arXiv 2611.25926) changes the training loop to counter this.
Standard GRPO samples \(G\) completions per prompt and normalizes rewards within the group:
\[\hat{A}_i = \frac{R_i - \text{mean}(R_{1:G})}{\text{std}(R_{1:G})}.\]

With binary rewards and a fraction \(p\) of completions correct, a correct sample gets advantage \(\sqrt{(1-p)/p}\) and an incorrect one gets \(-\sqrt{p/(1-p)}\). As \(p \to 1\), the positive advantage vanishes. When every completion is correct, the numerator is zero for all samples. Those prompts therefore contribute almost no learning signal, except that whatever gradient remains pushes probability further toward the already dominant mode.
ROAM-GRPO's mechanism, step by step:

1. Sample \(G\) completions per prompt and score them as usual.
2. Mark a prompt as solved if at least \(k\) of the \(G\) completions are correct.
3. Remove solved prompts from the GRPO objective.
4. Send them to an "off-mode" track, where the model is asked to produce distinct solution strategies.
5. Have an LLM judge check each candidate for logical validity and for distinctness from the others.
6. Self-distill the accepted alternatives back into the policy.
The brief doesn't give the distillation loss. The natural form is maximum likelihood on accepted samples \(y\) from the set \(\mathcal{A}(x)\):
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{distill}} = -\,\mathbb{E}_{x,\; y \in \mathcal{A}(x)} \big[\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\big].\]

Each prompt thus feeds either the RL term or the distillation term, never both. The threshold \(k\) sets the handoff point. A delayed variant, which enables this routing partway through training, is also reported.

This differs from the usual remedies for collapse. Entropy bonuses and KL regularization act on token-level randomness, which need not produce different strategies. Filtering out prompts whose groups are all correct or all wrong saves compute but discards the prompts rather than reusing them. Best-of-\(n\) or rejection-sampling distillation reinforces what the model already does. ROAM's distinguishing choice is to spend saturated prompts on a different objective, which rewards structural variety, with validity and distinctness enforced by a judge rather than by the verifier.

The authors' qualitative traces show baseline GRPO sticking to one dominant approach, while the ROAM variants try several, including some computational shortcuts. These are traces, not a measured diversity result. The paper is a short workshop submission, so the claims are preliminary.
Several open questions follow:

- **Judge reliability.** Distinctness is judged by an LLM, which may reward surface rephrasing or accept flawed reasoning. Self-distillation then bakes the judge's biases into the policy.
- **Inherited errors.** Alternatives on the off-mode track have no verifier guarantee, only a judge's opinion of validity. Shortcuts that work on the sampled problems could still be brittle elsewhere.
- **Measurement.** Evidence that diversity persists would need pass@\(k\) at large \(k\) or strategy-clustering metrics, not hand-picked traces.
- **Hyperparameters and cost.** The choice of \(k\) and the timing of the delayed switch are tuning knobs, and judge calls add overhead.
- **Interaction between objectives.** The distillation gradient could pull against the RL objective on shared parameters, and the paper's brief doesn't say how this is balanced.

articles.headline: K2-Horizon report details a 10T-synthetic-token pretraining recipe for a six-model open fleet
articles.dek: The Institute of Foundation Models (MBZUAI) published its 134-page technical report on models from 0.9B to a 375B-A23B MoE, with intermediate checkpoints and data pipelines.
body: K2-Horizon is a fleet of six open models. They run from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B mixture-of-experts flagship. The 3.7B, 7B, 32B and 36B-A4B models share one 22T-token corpus and recipe, which the authors say allows controlled studies of scale and sparsity. The 375B model trained on about 15T tokens in two phases, roughly 7.08T and then 8.05T, using newer data in phase 2.

The data recipe stands out. About 10T of the pretraining tokens are synthetic, in a web-heavy mix chosen by benchmark scores predicted at production scale. Agentic trajectories enter at context extension rather than only in post-training. IFM also reports nearly 17% of the corpus is explicit problem-solving trajectories. The 36B-A4B uses a new Mixture-of-Value-Attention (MoVA) design.

On benchmarks, the report says the 375B-A23B leads open-weight baselines on two evaluations and places second on eight more. Those baselines have 40–55B active parameters. One caveat: one coverage notes that data and code for the 375B and 36B-A4B models were still marked "will be released" at launch. That limits the openness claim for now.
articles.why: Releasing checkpoints, shared-recipe ablations, and synthetic-data pipelines makes pretraining and mid-training claims reproducible, which is rare at this scale.

terms.def: Sparse model routing each token to a few expert subnetworks.
Model-generated or rewritten text used as pretraining tokens.

sources.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models (arXiv)
MBZUAI Opens K2-Horizon Fleet, Six Models From 0.9B to 375B

deeper: K2-Horizon's main contribution is a data recipe, so start there. The report says about 10T of the pretraining tokens are synthetic, in a web-heavy mix. If that 10T refers to the 22T-token shared corpus, synthetic text is roughly 45% of it, though the brief does not say which corpus the figure applies to. Nearly 17% of the corpus is explicit problem-solving trajectories, so a large share of the signal is worked reasoning rather than raw prose.

The mixture is chosen by predicted benchmark score at production scale. The usual way to do this is to train many small proxy models on candidate mixtures \(w\) on the simplex \(\Delta\), fit a predictor \(\hat f\) of downstream score, and pick

\[
w^* = \arg\max_{w \in \Delta} \hat f(w; N_{\text{prod}}),
\]
where \(\hat f\) includes a scale-extrapolation term. A standard parametric form is the loss law

\[
L(N,D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}},
\]

with \(N\) the parameter count and \(D\) the token count. I am describing the generic method here, since the brief does not give the report's exact fitting procedure. The risk is that optimizing \(w\) against benchmark predictions also optimizes for benchmark-shaped data, which complicates any claim of generalization.

Agentic trajectories enter at context extension, not only in post-training. Long-context training is where multi-step tool use naturally fits, because a trajectory is a long sequence with sparse, delayed dependencies. Seeing these sequences during pretraining plausibly makes later post-training easier. This differs from the common pattern of pretraining on static text and adding agent behavior through supervised fine-tuning or RL.

The fleet design supports controlled comparison. The 3.7B, 7B, 32B and 36B-A4B models share one corpus and recipe. The 32B dense and 36B-A4B models are close in total parameters but differ sharply in active compute, which isolates the effect of sparsity. A mixture-of-experts layer computes

\[
y = \sum_{i \in \text{TopK}(g(x))} p_i(x)\, E_i(x), \qquad p = \text{softmax}(g(x)),
\]

so only \(k\) experts run per token. The 375B-A23B model activates about \(23/375 \approx 6\%\) of its parameters. With the standard estimate \(C \approx 6ND\) using active \(N\), training on about 15T tokens costs roughly \(6 \times 23\text{B} \times 15\text{T} \approx 2\times10^{24}\) FLOPs. The 375B run used two phases of about 7.08T and 8.05T tokens, with newer data in phase 2. The 36B-A4B also uses Mixture-of-Value-Attention (MoVA). The brief gives no mechanism for it, so I will not guess at one.

On results, the 375B-A23B leads open-weight baselines on two evaluations and places second on eight more. Those baselines have 40–55B active parameters. That is a favorable result per active parameter, and it matters for deployment because decode cost scales with active parameters, although the full 375B of weights must still sit in memory. The result is not a sweep, though.
Several questions remain open:
- **Attribution:** How much of the gain comes from synthetic data, from trajectory mix, and from sparsity? Ablations at production scale are expensive, and proxy-based selection may not trans

articles.headline: Best Probe Is Not the Best Steering Vector, New Study Finds
articles.dek: A UniReps@NeurIPS 2026 paper shows that the direction which best detects a concept in an LLM is not the one that best steers it.
body: Sadeghi and Becker study a common shortcut in activation engineering. A linear direction \(w\) in the residual stream is trained as a probe, then reused as a steering vector. <cite index="32-4">Probing reads \(w^\top h\), while steering adds a term proportional to \(\|h\|\,w\).</cite> The two operations use the same vector in different ways, so there is no guarantee that one optimum serves both.

The authors <cite index="31-6">build a one-parameter family of directions running from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference.</cite> They then compare probing and additive steering along that family at a fixed side effect. <cite index="31-5,31-7">In three instruction-tuned models from different families, on truthfulness and sentiment, steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference.</cite> The best probe is not the best steering direction in any of the models.

Transfer across models is also asymmetric. <cite index="32-8">Probes transfer more reliably than steering directions, and each role transfers well only under its own law.</cite> A concurrent preprint on safety behaviours found a similar read/write split, but it <cite index="34-5">reverses for sycophancy</cite>. That suggests the pattern depends on the data as well as the estimator.
articles.why: Steering vectors chosen for detection accuracy may be suboptimal, so interpretability pipelines should test the causal (write) role separately from the read role.

terms.def: Adding a scaled direction vector to hidden activations to shift model behavior.
Vector between class-conditional mean activations, ignoring covariance structure.

sources.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models? (arXiv:2611.19499)
Probing and Steering for Safety-Relevant Behaviours in Large Language Models

deeper: A common shortcut in activation engineering is to fit a linear direction \(w\) in the residual stream as a probe for some concept, then add it back as a steering vector. Sadeghi and Becker argue that this conflates two different operations. A probe reads the activation, producing a score \(w^\top h\). Steering writes to it, replacing \(h\) with
so the intervention is a displacement scaled by activation norm. Nothing ties the direction that is best for reading to the direction that is best for writing.

A simple argument shows why they can diverge. Let \(\Delta\mu = \mu_1-\mu_0\) be the difference of class-conditional means, and let \(\Sigma\) be the within-class covariance. A probe wants maximal class separation relative to noise, which is the Fisher criterion:

\[
\max_w \frac{(w^\top \Delta\mu)^2}{w^\top \Sigma w}\quad\Rightarrow\quad w \propto \Sigma^{-1}\Delta\mu .
\]
This is the linear discriminant direction. Steering at a fixed displacement magnitude instead wants to move the representation as far as possible along the concept axis:

\[
\max_{\|w\|=1} w^\top \Delta\mu \quad\Rightarrow\quad w \propto \Delta\mu .
\]

The discriminant direction tilts toward low-variance directions, because dividing by \(\Sigma\) amplifies them. These are good for reading, since they carry little noise. Pushing activations along them, however, may move the model off the distribution it was trained on. That is a plausible source of side effects, though it is my heuristic reading and not necessarily the authors' explanation.

The study makes this comparison systematic. It builds a one-parameter family of directions running from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference. One natural parameterization, which may differ from the paper's, is

\[
w_\lambda \propto \big((1-\lambda)\Sigma + \lambda I\big)^{-1}\Delta\mu,\qquad \lambda\in[0,1],
\]

which gives the discriminant at \(\lambda=0\) and the mean difference at \(\lambda=1\). Each direction is evaluated twice, as a probe and as an additive steering vector, with side effects held fixed for the steering runs. Across three instruction-tuned models from different families, on truthfulness and sentiment, steering consistently prefers directions nearer the mean difference. In none of the models is the best probe also the best steering direction.

This sits against two common practices. Contrastive mean-difference steering already works well in practice, but is usually justified empirically. Probe-derived steering, where a trained classifier's weights are reused as the intervention, implicitly assumes read and write optima coincide. The new result gives a reason to treat those as separate estimation problems.
Transfer across models

articles.headline: A Good Scaling-Law Fit Does Not Guarantee a Good Compute Prescription for Tabular Models
articles.dek: A Nov. 18 study of TabPFNv2-style foundation models finds that scaling-law fits can extrapolate poorly to unseen datasets.
body: Hog and colleagues ask whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style tabular foundation models <cite index="4-3">extrapolate reliably to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings.</cite> Their answer is cautious. The analysis <cite index="4-4">reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior. It also shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily give reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets.</cite>

These models are pretrained on synthetic data, so the data-generating process is itself a scaling axis. The authors report that <cite index="4-5">compute-optimal scaling requires widening the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute.</cite> <cite index="4-6">Raising the maximum rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and makes scaling trends more predictable.</cite>

The usual compute-optimal framing minimizes loss \(L(N,D)\) at a fixed compute budget \(C\). This result suggests that the fitted surface can be accurate in-distribution and still mislead the allocation between model size and data. It adds to other recent work showing that fitted exponents and error floors depend on the benchmark and setup.
articles.why: It is a reminder to validate scaling-law prescriptions out of distribution, and to treat pretraining-data diversity as a scaling variable alongside parameters and compute.

terms.def: Splitting a fixed compute budget between model size and data to minimize loss.
Pretrained transformer that does tabular prediction in-context, trained on synthetic datasets.

sources.title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models (arXiv:2611.24214)
Hinted Scaling Laws (arXiv:2611.02270)

deeper: A scaling law is usually validated by how well it predicts held-out loss at larger compute. Hog and colleagues point out that this is a weaker test than the one practitioners care about: whether the fitted law tells you how to spend compute on a dataset the fit never saw. For TabPFNv2-style models, their answer is that the two can diverge.

Start with the mechanism. These transformers are pretrained on a stream of synthetic datasets drawn from a prior over data-generating processes. At inference, a real table is supplied as context and the model predicts test labels in a single forward pass, approximating a posterior predictive. Pretraining therefore has more axes than in language modeling. Besides parameters \(N\) and training compute \(C\), the prior itself has knobs, notably the range of dataset sizes, meaning rows and features, that the generator samples.
The standard framing fits a parametric surface

\[
L(N,D) = E + A N^{-\alpha} + B D^{-\beta},
\]
and minimizes it under a budget. For dense transformers one often takes \(C \approx 6ND\). Substituting \(D = C/(6N)\) and setting \(\partial L/\partial N = 0\) gives

\[
N^*(C) \propto C^{\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}}, \qquad D^*(C) \propto C^{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}}.
\]

The prescription depends on the ratio of the fitted exponents, not on the loss value. Small errors in \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) barely change predicted loss over the fitted range, but they shift the allocation exponent \(\beta/(\alpha+\beta)\) and compound when extrapolated. Near the optimum the surface is also flat, so many allocations have nearly equal fitted loss. The argmin is ill-conditioned even when the surface is accurate.

The tabular case adds a second problem. The fit is made on synthetic pretraining loss or a particular benchmark, while the target is real tables. If the exponents and floor \(E\) differ between synthetic and real behavior, as the authors report, the surface can be accurate in-distribution and still misallocate between size and data on unseen datasets. A natural extension is to treat the prior's range as a variable \(S\), writing \(L(N,D,S)\). The reported finding is that compute-optimal scaling requires widening the range of synthetic dataset sizes along with model size and compute. Raising the maximum rows and features sampled in pretraining improves performance and makes trends more predictable. A narrow prior probably makes the extrapolation target a moving one, because gains saturate for reasons unrelated to \(N\) or \(D\).

Compared with language-model scaling analyses, where the data distribution is fixed and the evaluation distribution is close to it, tabular foundation models have a pretraining distribution that the designer chooses. The "data" term \(D\) is thus not just a count. It depends on the diversity and extent of the generator, so a single-exponent \(D\) term is a misspecification.

Several limitations and open questions remain. The prescription's sensitivity should be quantified, for instance with confidence regions on \(N^*(C)\) from bootstrap refits rather than point estimates. It is unclear whether a joint law over \((N,D,S)\) is stable or whether interactions between the prior's range and model size break separability. Evaluation also matters. This work adds to other recent results showing that fitted exponents and error floors depend on the benchmark and setup, so reported exponents are conditional on the experimental design. Finally, the approximation \(C\approx 6ND\) may not describe attention over rows and features, whose cost grows with table size, so the budget constraint itself may need to be modeled.

articles.headline: Thinking Machines ships Inkling 2 Mini, an open looped MoE sized for a laptop
articles.dek: The 26.4B-parameter Apache 2.0 model reruns its middle layers three times per token, which trades extra compute for a small memory footprint.
body: <cite index="23-1">Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026, as open weights under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face.</cite> <cite index="23-2">It is a 24-layer decoder-only MoE. The middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, which gives 48 layer applications from 24 layers of weights. Each layer routes every token to 8 of 128 experts.</cite>

<cite index="23-3">The model has 26.4B total and 3.4B active parameters. Each extra loop pass adds about 1.0B effective parameters, so three passes give 5.4B effective active parameters per token.</cite> In effect, \(N_{\text{eff}} \approx N_{\text{active}} + (L-1)\,\Delta\) with \(L=3\) and \(\Delta\approx 1.0\)B. <cite index="23-5">Most weights are trained and deployed natively in NVFP4, and the last 4 layers use MXFP8. The total footprint is about 20GB.</cite> <cite index="28-6">That is small enough for a 32GB Mac or a single NVIDIA DGX Spark.</cite>

Reported results are self-reported. <cite index="28-11,28-12">The model scores 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Index, tied with Qwen3.8-27B, and 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only).</cite> <cite index="28-13">Its weakest results are 15.2% on HLE-Diamond and 50.0% on MultiChallenge.</cite> The lab also released a variable-loop research checkpoint. <cite index="21-11">It says chain of thought gets shorter at this scale but stays legible, with no meaningful drop in monitorability.</cite>
articles.why: Looping adds depth without adding weights, so it is a way to spend inference compute instead of memory on local agent hardware.

terms.def: Reuses a block of shared layers several times per token to deepen computation.
NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point format with block scaling, used here for training and serving.

sources.title: Introducing Inkling 2 Mini - Thinking Machines Lab
Meet Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Mini: 26B Looped MoE Runs on a 32GB Mac - MarkTechPost

deeper: Inkling 2 Mini combines two ways of getting more computation per parameter: sparse expert routing and weight-tied depth recurrence. It is a 24-layer decoder-only transformer. The middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, so the network applies 48 layers from 24 layers of weights. Every layer routes each token to 8 of 128 experts.
Write the model as a prelude \(P\), a looped block \(B\), and a coda \(C\). Then

\[
h^{(0)} = P(x), \qquad h^{(\ell+1)} = B\big(h^{(\ell)}\big),\ \ \ell = 0,1,2, \qquad y = C\big(h^{(3)}\big).
\]
Inside each layer the MoE feed-forward computes

\[
\text{MoE}(u) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(u)} g_i(u)\, E_i(u), \qquad |\mathcal{T}(u)| = 8,
\]

where \(\mathcal{T}(u)\) is the top-8 set chosen from router logits over 128 experts, and \(g_i\) are normalized gate weights. Only 1/16 of expert capacity fires per token. Active parameters are 3.4B of 26.4B total, about 13%, because attention and embeddings are dense.
The lab's accounting for the extra passes is

articles.headline: Quantizing only the draft model's KV cache cuts speculative-decoding memory by two-thirds
articles.dek: A NeurIPS 2026 workshop paper finds that 4-bit keys and values in the draft cache barely change acceptance rates.
body: Two-model speculative decoding needs a second KV cache for the draft model. <cite index="11-1,11-2">A new paper from Saksham Gupta and Michael Li quantizes that draft cache. It follows KIVI with K4V4 quantization: per-channel keys and per-token values.</cite> <cite index="12-4">The target cache and verifier stay in BF16.</cite> Verification is unchanged, so the output distribution is preserved.

The authors argue that key and value precision cannot be chosen independently of the quantizer layout. <cite index="11-2,11-3">With a naive per-token quantizer, K8V4 beat K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87 percentage points. With grouped per-channel keys, the gap became -0.25 points.</cite> That matters because expected tokens per verification step grows with the acceptance rate \(\alpha\) and draft length \(\gamma\) as \(\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}\).

<cite index="11-5,11-6">Across six model pairs, draft cache memory fell 66.20% and combined memory across both caches fell 23.95%. Mean acceptance dropped from 57.93% to 57.14%.</cite> <cite index="19-8">At 16K and 32K context with the Qwen2.5 3B/1.5B pair, combined KV memory fell by about 31%.</cite> <cite index="12-10">The experiments use greedy decoding at batch size one</cite>, so throughput under production load remains untested.
articles.why: KV memory limits concurrency and context length in serving, so shrinking the draft cache frees capacity without changing the verified output.

terms.def: Cached attention keys and values held by the small speculative-drafting model.
Fraction of drafted tokens the target model accepts during verification.

sources.title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache (arXiv)
Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache (HTML)

deeper: Two-model speculative decoding runs a small draft model for \(\gamma\) tokens, then has the large target model score them in one forward pass. The cost is that the draft model needs its own KV cache next to the target's. This paper quantizes only the draft cache, using the KIVI recipe at 4 bits for both keys and values (K4V4). Keys are quantized per channel and values per token. The target cache and the verifier stay in BF16.

Quantization error in the draft is cheap because it only perturbs the proposal distribution \(q\). Verification still accepts a drafted token \(x\) with probability \(\min\left(1, p(x)/q(x)\right)\), where \(p\) is the target distribution, and resamples from the residual on rejection. That procedure yields samples from \(p\) for any \(q\), so a worse draft costs speed, not correctness. Under greedy decoding the output is simply the target's argmax sequence. Speed depends on the acceptance rate \(\alpha\). If each token is accepted independently with probability \(\alpha\), the expected tokens produced per verification step is

\[
\mathbb{E}[N] = \sum_{i=0}^{\gamma} \alpha^i = \frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha},
\]
which tends to \(\gamma+1\) as \(\alpha \to 1\). The aim is therefore to cut memory while holding \(\alpha\) nearly fixed.
The quantizer is asymmetric uniform, applied per group:

\[
\hat{x} = s\,\mathrm{round}\!\left(\frac{x-z}{s}\right)+z,\qquad s=\frac{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}{2^b-1}.
\]

Layout determines which elements share \((s,z)\). Key activations have a few outlier channels. A per-token quantizer shares one scale across all channels, so the outliers stretch the range and crush the rest. Grouping per channel isolates the outliers. Values lack that channel structure, so per-token grouping works for them.

The authors' main claim is that key and value precision cannot be chosen independently of this layout. With a naive per-token quantizer, K8V4 beat K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87 percentage points, so key precision seemed to be what mattered. With grouped per-channel keys the gap became -0.25 points, so 4-bit keys were no longer the bottleneck. The earlier conclusion reflected the quantizer, not an intrinsic key sensitivity.

articles.headline: Point Dynamics Proxy Gives Robot World Models a Physics Stage Before the Pixels
articles.dek: A Nov. 19 paper splits robotic video prediction into 3D point simulation and rendering, and reports lower object-motion error on DROID.
body: Robotic world models usually predict future frames from the current observation and an action sequence. The authors argue that this conditioning says where the robot goes but not how the scene reacts. That forces a single video model to infer interaction dynamics implicitly while it also renders appearance.

Their fix is a proxy. <cite index="14-4">They lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how those points respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read.</cite> The dynamics model is therefore separate from the renderer. In the notation of the abstract, the dynamics step is roughly \(P_{t+1} = g_\phi(P_t, a_t)\), and the video model is conditioned on a rendering of \(P_{1:T}\).

<cite index="14-5">On DROID, with two video renderers of different architectures, the proxy cut object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without hurting image quality. On a real bimanual robot the reduction was 8.1%.</cite> These are modest gains. They do suggest that improving the dynamics module alone can make a world model more faithful.
articles.why: It shows that factoring dynamics from appearance can improve action-conditioned video world models without retraining the renderer, which matters for using them as policy evaluators and data generators.

terms.def: Learned network predicting how 3D scene points move in response to robot actions.
Large real-world robot manipulation dataset used here to evaluate video world models.

sources.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models (arXiv:2611.25946)

deeper: Most robotic world models learn a mapping from the current observation \(o_1\) and an action sequence \(a_{1:T}\) to future frames, \(p(o_{2:T} \mid o_1, a_{1:T})\). The authors' complaint is that actions say where the robot goes but not how the scene responds. A single video model must therefore learn contact, occlusion, and object motion implicitly, while also generating textures and lighting. Both jobs share one set of weights and one pixel-space loss.

Their remedy splits the problem into stages. First, the initial frame is lifted into a 3D point set \(P_1\). The brief doesn't say how, but the usual route is monocular depth plus camera intrinsics, back-projecting each pixel \((u,v)\) with depth \(d\) as \(x = d\,K^{-1}[u,v,1]^\top\). Second, a learned point dynamics model rolls the points forward under the robot's motion:

\[
P_{t+1} = g_\phi(P_t, a_t), \qquad t = 1,\dots,T-1.
\]

Third, the simulated trajectory \(P_{1:T}\) is rendered back into the image plane, producing pixel-aligned conditioning videos \(\tilde{o}_{1:T} = R(P_{1:T})\). Finally, any video model is conditioned on that rendering, and its job reduces to turning a coarse, geometrically consistent depiction into a realistic one.
Probabilistically, this replaces one conditional with a factorization:

\[
p(o_{2:T}\mid o_1,a_{1:T}) \approx \int p\big(o_{2:T}\mid R(P_{1:T}),\,o_1\big)\; p\big(P_{1:T}\mid P_1,a_{1:T}\big)\, dP_{1:T}.
\]

The dynamics term is trained on point trajectories, which is a lower-dimensional target than pixels. Because \(R\) is a deterministic projection, the proxy lines up spatially with the video model's output, so it can act as dense conditioning rather than a latent code. That is why the renderer's architecture can vary.

This differs from two common alternatives. Action-conditioned video diffusion or autoregressive models inject \(a_t\) as embeddings and hope physics emerges. Explicit simulators, by contrast, require known geometry, masses, and contact parameters, and they are hard to apply to unstructured scenes. The proxy sits between them: the dynamics are learned but live in an explicit 3D state space that is easier to supervise and inspect than latents.

On DROID, using two video renderers of different architectures, object motion error fell by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality. On a real bimanual robot, the reduction was 8.1%. These gains are modest, but the same dynamics module helps different renderers, which supports the claim that dynamics is a separable bottleneck.

Several questions remain. Rollouts of \(g_\phi\) are autoregressive, so errors in \(P_t\) compound, and a bad point trajectory will be rendered faithfully as a bad video. Lifting a single frame into points inherits depth errors, and it handles occluded or unseen geometry poorly. A point set may not capture deformables, liquids, or articulated constraints well, and the brief doesn't say how \(g_\phi\) is structured for these cases. The deterministic form \(P_{t+1}=g_\phi(P_t,a_t)\) also leaves out stochastic outcomes, such as whether a grasp slips. Finally, "object motion error" measures only part of fidelity, so it is worth checking whether the improvements carry over to downstream uses like policy evaluation or planning, where the true test of a world model lies.

articles.headline: Audit of ANYmal D Learned Simulator Finds Prediction Accuracy Doesn't Predict Walking
articles.dek: A Nov. 17 CPU-only replication of the Robotic World Model shows that better multi-step prediction can still produce failing policies.
body: The Robotic World Model (RWM) is a neural dynamics model that a legged robot can use as a learned simulator, with the network rolled forward on its own predictions: \(\hat{s}_{t+1} = f_\theta(\hat{s}_t, a_t)\). A new audit examines the ANYmal D quadruped version and the uncertainty estimate from its follow-up, RWM-U. <cite index="15-4">The author rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly. They measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures.</cite>

Policies trained inside these simulators were then tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. The headline result is a mismatch between prediction accuracy and control quality. <cite index="15-5">All 18 fine-tuned copies predicted better than the released model, one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies.</cite>

The abstract also says that registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by the policies they produce were not settled. The practical lesson is to validate learned simulators on downstream policy outcomes, not on rollout error. The audit's results come from one published system on one platform.
articles.why: It is a caution for the world-model-as-simulator pipeline: held-out prediction error is a weak proxy for whether policies trained in the model will transfer.

terms.def: Neural network simulator of robot dynamics, rolled out autoregressively to train policies.
RWM follow-up adding uncertainty estimates for offline model-based reinforcement learning.

sources.title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D (arXiv:2611.23118)

deeper: The Robotic World Model treats a neural network as a stand-in for a physics engine. Given a state estimate and an action, it predicts the next state, and at rollout time it consumes its own output:

\[
\hat{s}_{t+1} = f_\theta(\hat{s}_t, a_t), \qquad \hat{s}_0 = s_0 .
\]

A policy is then trained by reinforcement learning entirely inside this loop, with rewards computed on the imagined states. The audit asks whether the usual evidence that such a simulator is good, low prediction error, actually tells you the resulting policy will walk.
The mechanism runs in four steps. First, fit \(f_\theta\) to logged robot data by minimizing a prediction loss, for example

\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\big\|f_\theta(s_t,a_t)-s_{t+1}\big\|^2,
\]

or a multi-step variant that unrolls on its own predictions to reduce compounding error. Second, optimize a policy against the imagined return \(\hat J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\hat\tau\sim(f_\theta,\pi)}\big[\sum_t\gamma^t r(\hat s_t,a_t)\big]\). Third, optionally use an uncertainty estimate, as in RWM-U, to discount rewards where the model is unreliable, \(\tilde r = r-\lambda\,u(\hat s,a)\). Fourth, deploy the policy. Here the authors tested it in a hand-built MuJoCo model of ANYmal D.

The central problem is distribution shift. Rollout metrics average error over the data distribution \(d_{\mathcal D}\), but the policy optimizer seeks states where the model is wrong in its favor. The return gap

depends on error along the policy's own state-visitation distribution \(d^{\pi}\), which the optimizer actively shapes. A model can lower average error at one and eight steps while becoming more exploitable in the narrow regions the policy cares about. Because \(\pi\) is chosen by \(\arg\max\) against \(f_\theta\), small, structured errors matter more than the mean.

The audit makes this concrete. The author rebuilt the model to reproduce the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, then measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures. All 18 fine-tuned copies predicted better than the released model at one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 produced failing policies. Better accuracy did not imply better control.

Compared with earlier approaches, this sits in the lineage of Dyna-style model-based RL, where short model rollouts supplement real data, and of uncertainty-penalized methods that keep the policy near well-modeled regions. It differs from hand-built physics simulators, whose errors are structured (contact parameters, actuator models) and can be inspected and randomized. Learned simulators trade that interpretability for fidelity to real data, but the audit suggests the fidelity may be measured in the wrong currency.

Several limitations matter. The results come from one published system on one platform, so they may not transfer to other robots or architectures. The MuJoCo test model is hand-built and is itself an imperfect proxy for hardware. The abstract also says that registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by the policies they produce were not settled. So no cheap proxy is yet shown to replace policy-level evaluation, and it remains open whether the uncertainty estimate helps. The practical rule is to validate learned simulators on downstream policy outcomes, not

articles.headline: AlphaGenome 2 scores DNA variants cell type by cell type, and roughly doubles causal-variant recall in DeepMind's own benchmark
articles.dek: Google DeepMind's November 11 preprint conditions a genome sequence model on cell identity and reports about twice the recall of its predecessor for causal single-cell eQTLs, but the numbers are unreviewed and come from DeepMind itself.
body: On November 11, 2026, Google DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2, with a technical preprint (also posted to bioRxiv). The model predicts for one tissue, cell type or cell state per call instead of thousands of tracks at once. Nature reports it was trained on single-cell gene-activity and other measurements from more than 100 million cells across 68 tissues. A cell encoder can turn a researcher's own single-cell RNA-seq data into a condition, so predictions for new disease states need no further fine-tuning, according to coverage of the paper. Nature says the model was trained on 637 human and 311 mouse cell types.

The headline benchmark is TenK10K, a single-cell eQTL map of 28 primary immune cell types. At 90% precision, DeepMind reports that AlphaGenome 2 recovered 30% of putatively causal variants, against 16% for the original model fine-tuned on single-cell data. It also reports 43% recall at 90% sign accuracy for effect direction, against 23%. Qualitatively, the model reproduced key aspects of a 2024 inflammatory bowel disease finding. It singled out the variant and predicted that it boosts ETS2 in gut macrophages while leaving other cell types largely unaffected. This was an in silico reproduction of a known wet-lab result, not a new experimental discovery. In another test it was given single-cell data from a COVID-19 mRNA vaccine study it had not seen. It separated activated from resting T cells and predicted a stronger effect for a severe-COVID-associated variant in the activated state.
articles.why: Pinpointing which variant acts in which cell is the bottleneck between GWAS hits and drug targets, and conditioning on cell state is a concrete architectural step toward that.

terms.def: Genetic variant associated with a change in a gene's expression level.
Statistical method assigning causal probabilities to correlated variants within an association signal.

sources.title: Nature News: DeepMind's ultra-powerful AI for genome mapping wows scientists
AlphaGenome 2 predicts regulatory activity and variant effects across cell states (bioRxiv preprint)
Google DeepMind: AlphaGenome 2 blog post
Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions (bioRxiv)
Chemistry World: Sequel to AlphaGenome predicts how small DNA changes affect cells
Implicator.ai: AlphaGenome 2 Predicts DNA Variant Effects by Cell Type
Advancing regulatory variant effect prediction with AlphaGenome (Nature, PMC)

background: Genome-wide association studies link thousands of genomic regions to traits, but most signals sit in non-coding DNA. A signal usually covers many correlated variants, and the causal one can act only in a particular cell type or cell state. Schematically, a sequence model \(f_\theta\) is asked for the effect of a variant \(v\) on gene \(g\) in context \(c\): \[\Delta_g(v,c)=f_\theta(x^{\text{alt}},c)_g-f_\theta(x^{\text{ref}},c)_g.\] The ground truth is statistical, not experimental. Fine-mapping assigns posterior probabilities to variants being causal for expression changes (eQTLs). Models are then scored on how many of these "putatively causal" variants they recover at a fixed precision. A tissue-averaged prediction can dilute a signal that exists in only one cell population.

The original AlphaGenome (Avsec et al., Nature 649, 2026) unified multimodal prediction, long-sequence context and base-pair resolution in one model. It reported state-of-the-art results on 22 of 24 genome-track tasks and 25 of 26 variant-effect tasks. Its design still predicted many tissue-level tracks at once. A bioRxiv preprint from early November (DOI dated November 6) tested that original model on 2,111 promoter-gene pairs disrupted in silico. It found that the model recognized the local loss of promoter activity but often failed to carry the effect through to the rest of the gene's transcript.
articles.status: The results come from a non-peer-reviewed DeepMind preprint with no independent evaluation of version 2 reported yet, although outside scientists quoted by Chemistry World were positive and the earlier AlphaGenome paper was peer-reviewed in Nature.
deeper: AlphaGenome 2 changes the conditioning of the model more than its core task. The original model read a DNA window and emitted thousands of tissue-level tracks at once. The new one is queried for a single context per call, so the function is \(f_\theta(x, c)\), where \(c\) denotes a tissue, cell type or cell state. The variant effect is still the alternate-minus-reference difference:
\[\Delta_g(v,c)=f_\theta(x^{\text{alt}},c)_g-f_\theta(x^{\text{ref}},c)_g.\]

The mechanism, step by step, as reported. Training used single-cell gene-activity and other measurements from more than 100 million cells across 68 tissues, covering 637 human and 311 mouse cell types. A cell encoder maps a researcher's own single-cell RNA-seq data to a condition vector, roughly \(c=E_\phi(\text{scRNA-seq})\). Because \(c\) is computed rather than looked up in a fixed vocabulary of labels, a new disease state can in principle be handled at inference time with no fine-tuning. The coverage I have does not describe the encoder's architecture or how it is trained, so I won't guess.

The context-specific design matters because of dilution. If a variant acts in one population with effect \(\delta\) and that population has weight \(w\) in a mixture, a tissue-averaged readout sees about \(w\delta\), which can fall below the model's noise floor. Conditioning on the right cell state avoids the averaging.

The evaluation is statistical. Fine-mapping gives each eQTL variant a posterior probability of being causal, and variants above some threshold are labelled "putatively causal." A score threshold \(\tau\) is then chosen so that precision hits 90%, and the reported number is
\[\text{recall}=\frac{|\{v:\ |\Delta_g(v,c)|>\tau\}\cap \mathcal{C}|}{|\mathcal{C}|},\]

where \(\mathcal{C}\) is the putatively causal set. Direction is scored separately: recall at 90% sign accuracy, where \(\operatorname{sign}\Delta_g\) must match the eQTL effect direction. On TenK10K, a single-cell eQTL map of 28 primary immune cell types, DeepMind reports 30% recall against 16% for the original model fine-tuned on single-cell data, and 43% against 23% for direction. Both roughly double.

Against prior approaches, the original unified multimodal prediction, long context and base-pair resolution, but predicted many tissue tracks jointly. A preprint tested that model on 2,111 promoter-gene pairs disrupted in silico. It found the model recognized the local loss of promoter activity but often failed to propagate the effect to the rest of the transcript. The new design addresses a different failure, cell-type dilution, so it is not clear that it fixes the propagation problem.

Several limitations apply. The benchmark and the comparison come from DeepMind itself, and the baseline is the earlier model fine-tuned rather than an independent method. The labels are fine-mapped statistical calls, not experimental measurements. They inherit linkage-disequilibrium ambiguity and are noisy, so "recall" measures agreement with a proxy. Even at the reported numbers, most putatively causal variants are missed at 90% precision. TenK10K covers immune cells only, so generalization to other tissues is untested here. The inflammatory bowel disease result, in which the model singled out the variant and predicted higher ETS2 in gut macrophages with little effect elsewhere, reproduces a known 2024 wet-lab finding and is not new discovery. The COVID-19 vaccine test is suggestive. The model separated activated from resting T cells and predicted a stronger effect for a severe-COVID-associated variant in the activated state. Without experimental validation, though, it is a plausibility check. Open questions include how well the encoder handles states far from its training distribution, whether predictions are calibrated, and whether transcript-level propagation has improved.

articles.headline: The Transformer Revisited: Attention as a Soft Dictionary Lookup
articles.dek: Attention replaces a hard key-value lookup with a differentiable, similarity-weighted average, and that one move underlies nearly every frontier language model.
body: A dictionary maps a query to the value whose key matches exactly. Attention relaxes this: the query is compared with every key, and the output is a weighted blend of all values, with weights from a softmax over similarities. Because the lookup is soft, it is differentiable, so what to retrieve is learned end to end. This removed the recurrent bottleneck. An RNN squeezes history into one fixed-size state and must process tokens sequentially. Attention gives every token a direct, constant-depth path to every other token and trains in parallel across the sequence.

Stack token representations into a matrix \(X\) (one row per token) and project them as \(Q=XW_Q\), \(K=XW_K\), \(V=XW_V\), where \(d_k\) is the key/query dimension. Then:
\[\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right)V\]\nThe \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) factor keeps dot-product variance near one (assuming roughly unit-variance entries), so the softmax does not saturate and kill gradients. \(M\) is a causal mask (\(-\infty\) above the diagonal, 0 elsewhere) for autoregressive models. Multi-head attention runs several such lookups in parallel subspaces and concatenates them. With sequence length \(n\) and model width \(d\), the cost is \(O(n^2 d)\) compute and, naively, \(O(n^2)\) memory. FlashAttention reduces memory traffic by tiling, without changing the math. At inference, a KV cache stores past keys and values so each new token costs \(O(nd)\) attention compute per layer instead of a full recomputation, but the cache grows with layers, heads, and context.

Today's frontier and open-weight models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek) are mostly decoder-only transformers with pre-normalization and rotary position embeddings. Much of the recent engineering targets the KV cache. Grouped-query attention shares key/value heads across query heads, and DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent. Sliding-window or interleaved local/global layers cap the quadratic cost on long contexts. Mixture-of-experts feed-forward blocks add capacity without proportional compute, and some hybrids mix in state-space layers. The core lookup is unchanged, and the variations mostly manage its memory and bandwidth costs.
articles.why: Nearly every modern architecture choice, from GQA to long-context tricks, is a response to the cost profile of this one primitive.

terms.def: Stored past keys and values reused to avoid recomputation during autoregressive decoding.
Several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache.
Additive mask preventing tokens from attending to future positions.

sources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)
Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate (Bahdanau et al., 2014)

deeper: Start with a hash map: a query is matched against stored keys, and the value under the one exact match is returned. Attention relaxes this into a soft lookup. For token \(i\), the query \(q_i\) is scored against every key \(k_j\), the scores are normalized with a softmax, and the output is the resulting weighted average of the values:
\[\alpha_{ij}=\frac{\exp(q_i^\top k_j/\sqrt{d_k})}{\sum_{l}\exp(q_i^\top k_l/\sqrt{d_k})},\qquad o_i=\sum_j \alpha_{ij}\,v_j .\]

As the scores become sharply peaked, this approaches a hard dictionary lookup. Because the weights are a smooth function of the scores, gradients flow through the retrieval, so what to look up, and what to store as keys and values, is learned end to end.
In matrix form, the token representations form \(X\), with one row per token. Three learned projections give \(Q=XW_Q\), \(K=XW_K\), \(V=XW_V\), and the whole layer is
\[\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right)V .\]

The product \(QK^\top\) is an \(n\times n\) matrix of all pairwise similarities. The softmax acts row-wise. The mask \(M\) holds \(-\infty\) above the diagonal, so a token cannot attend to its future and the model stays autoregressive. The \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) factor matters numerically. If query and key entries have roughly unit variance, an unscaled dot product has variance about \(d_k\). Large logits would saturate the softmax into near one-hot outputs with vanishing gradients. Scaling brings the variance back near one. Multi-head attention runs several of these lookups in separate learned subspaces and concatenates the results, letting different heads retrieve different relations.

The comparison with recurrence is about information paths and parallelism. An RNN compresses all history into one fixed-size state and must step through tokens in order, so distant information has to survive many sequential transformations. Attention gives each token a direct, constant-depth connection to every other token, and all positions are computed at once during training, which maps well onto accelerators.

The price is cost. Compute is \(O(n^2 d)\) for sequence length \(n\) and width \(d\), and a naive implementation materializes the \(n\times n\) score matrix, using \(O(n^2)\) memory. FlashAttention leaves the math unchanged but tiles the computation to cut memory traffic. At inference, a KV cache keeps past keys and values, so each new token costs \(O(nd)\) attention compute per layer rather than a full recomputation. The catch is that the cache grows with layers, heads, and context length, and in long-context serving it often becomes the binding constraint.

Much current work therefore targets the cache rather than the lookup itself. Grouped-query attention shares key/value heads across groups of query heads. Multi-head latent attention, used by DeepSeek, stores a low-rank latent from which keys and values are reconstructed. Sliding-window or interleaved local/global layers bound the quadratic term. Mixture-of-experts feed-forward blocks add parameters without proportional compute, and some hybrids insert state-space layers. The open-weight families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek) are mostly decoder-only, pre-normalized, and use rotary position embeddings.

Open questions follow from these trade-offs. Compression and locality save memory but risk losing information that a full lookup could retrieve, and how much that matters at very long context is hard to settle. Hybrids with state-space layers reintroduce a fixed-size state, so the old bottleneck returns in a milder form. The central tension remains: the soft lookup is expressive and parallel, but exact all-pairs retrieval is expensive, and most architectural variation is a negotiation with that cost.

articles.headline: Hopfield Networks: Memory as a Ball Rolling Downhill
articles.dek: Hopfield's 1982 paper recast recall as energy minimization in a recurrent network, so a corrupted input settles into the nearest stored pattern.
body: In the early 1980s, computers stored memories by address: you needed to know where something lived to retrieve it. Biological memory works differently. A fragment of a face or a few notes of a tune pulls up the whole. Hopfield's 1982 PNAS paper, "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities," asked whether such content-addressable recall could emerge from many simple interacting units, with no central controller, by borrowing ideas from the physics of interacting systems.

The model is a set of \(N\) binary units \(s_i \in \{-1,+1\}\) with symmetric weights \(w_{ij}=w_{ji}\) and no self-connections (\(w_{ii}=0\)). To store patterns \(\xi^\mu\), \(\mu=1,\dots,P\), a Hebbian outer-product rule sets \(w_{ij}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}\xi_i^\mu \xi_j^\mu\) for \(i\neq j\). Each unit is updated asynchronously by a threshold rule: \(s_i \leftarrow \operatorname{sgn}\big(\sum_j w_{ij}s_j-\theta_i\big)\). The key insight is that this dynamics has a Lyapunov function, an energy:
\[ E(\mathbf{s}) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i\neq j} w_{ij}\, s_i s_j + \sum_i \theta_i s_i \]

Here \(\theta_i\) is the threshold of unit \(i\). Because the weights are symmetric, flipping a unit according to the update rule changes the energy by \(\Delta E = -\Delta s_i\big(\sum_j w_{ij}s_j-\theta_i\big)\le 0\), where \(\Delta s_i\) is the new value of \(s_i\) minus the old one. Energy never rises, so the state must settle in a local minimum. Stored patterns sit near these minima, which act as attractors, and a noisy or partial cue falls into the basin of a nearby memory. The price is limited capacity: the number of reliably stored patterns grows only linearly with \(N\), and overloading the network creates spurious mixture states.

Hopfield's framing influenced later work on energy-based models, Boltzmann-style stochastic networks, and the use of statistical physics to analyze learning. Its most striking recent echo is in attention. Modern Hopfield variants replace the quadratic energy with sharper, exponential-type interactions, giving continuous states and far higher capacity. Their one-step retrieval, \(\xi_{\text{new}} = X\,\operatorname{softmax}(\beta X^{\top}\xi)\), where the columns of \(X\) are stored patterns, \(\xi\) is the query state, and \(\beta\) is an inverse temperature, has the same form as softmax attention over keys and values. In that view a transformer attention layer performs associative lookup, a descendant of the 1982 idea.
articles.why: It gave neural computation a clean energy-landscape view of memory, one that still shapes how we analyze retrieval, capacity, and attention.

deeper: Before Hopfield's 1982 PNAS paper, "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities," the standard model of computer memory was lookup by address. Hopfield asked whether content-addressable recall, where a fragment retrieves the whole, could emerge from many simple interacting units with no central controller.
The mechanism has three steps. First, the state is a vector \(\mathbf{s}\in\{-1,+1\}^N\). Second, patterns \(\xi^\mu\), \(\mu=1,\dots,P\), are stored in the weights by the Hebbian outer-product rule
\[ w_{ij}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\xi_i^\mu\xi_j^\mu \quad (i\neq j),\qquad w_{ii}=0, \]
which makes \(w_{ij}=w_{ji}\). Third, recall starts from a noisy or partial cue and updates one randomly chosen unit at a time:
\[ s_i \leftarrow \operatorname{sgn}\Big(\sum_j w_{ij}s_j-\theta_i\Big), \]
where \(\theta_i\) is the threshold of unit \(i\).
The key result is that this dynamics descends an energy,
\[ E(\mathbf{s})=-\tfrac12\sum_{i\neq j}w_{ij}s_is_j+\sum_i\theta_i s_i . \]
Only terms containing \(s_i\) change when unit \(i\) flips. Symmetry of \(w\) means the factor \(\tfrac12\) cancels against the double counting of pairs, giving
\[ \Delta E=-\Delta s_i\Big(\sum_j w_{ij}s_j-\theta_i\Big)\le 0, \]

with \(\Delta s_i\) the new value minus the old. A flip occurs only when \(\Delta s_i\) has the same sign as the local field, so the product is nonnegative. Since \(E\) is bounded on a finite state space and never rises, the dynamics must reach a local minimum. The ball-rolling-downhill picture follows: minima are attractors, and a cue inside a basin rolls to the associated memory.

Why stored patterns sit near minima: with \(\theta_i=0\) and a single stored pattern, \(\sum_{j}w_{ij}\xi_j=\frac{N-1}{N}\xi_i\), so the pattern is a fixed point. With \(P\) patterns, the field on unit \(i\) is the signal from the target pattern plus crosstalk from the others. That crosstalk behaves like noise whose size grows with \(P/N\), which is the origin of the capacity limit.

Compared with address-based memory, nothing here is stored in a location. Information is distributed across all weights, retrieval tolerates corruption, and computation is local. The costs are real. Capacity scales only linearly in \(N\), and the network stores far fewer bits than a conventional memory of similar size. Overloading produces spurious attractors, including mixtures of stored patterns. Because \(E\) is even in \(\mathbf{s}\) when \(\theta=0\), the negation \(-\xi^\mu\) is also an attractor. Descent guarantees only a local minimum, not the correct one. The convergence proof also needs symmetric weights and asynchronous updates, and symmetry is a doubtful assumption for biological circuits.
